bull_thesis: Sallie Mae is the dominant US private student lender trading at about 7.3 times trailing earnings (roughly $3.57 of earnings per share against a $26 stock) with a legislated growth runway the trailing numbers cannot yet show. Layered on top is a deliberate pivot to a more capital-light, fee-based model: the KKR forward-flow partnership buys newly originated loans for a gain plus recurring program-management and servicing fees (fee revenue up more than 50% year-over-year off a small base). Capital allocation is a genuine edge - roughly 59% of shares retired since 2020 at an average of about $17, with management leaning in counter-cyclically (a $200M accelerated repurchase near $21.50 in Q1 2026). Underwriting is improving into the growth push, not loosening (cosigner rate ~95%, average approval FICO ~755). Returns are high (ROE ~34%) and capital is strong (CET1 11.8%). If the PLUS ramp converts and net interest margin recovers from its 4.75% Q2 trough toward the ~5% management targets, earnings per share can inflect toward the 'high teens to low 20s' growth management has floated for 2027, supporting a re-rate. Conditions the bull case needs: PLUS-reform originations actually captured this peak season, net interest margin normalizing, and consumer credit holding.
bear_thesis: This is a late-cycle consumer-credit lender whose reported growth is largely manufactured. Five-year earnings-per-share compound growth is negative (-1.1%); EPS only just returned near its 2021 level, and the rise is powered by a ~59% cut in the share count and by lumpy gains on loan sales, not organic compounding. The most recent quarter exposed the fragility: Q2 2026 GAAP EPS was just $0.29, missing the ~$0.46 consensus, with net interest income down $44M year-over-year and margin at a 4.75% trough. Credit is turning at the margin - net charge-offs rose to $113M from $94M a year earlier, and a new default channel (third-party 'debt resolution' firms pushing able borrowers straight to default) cost ~$16M and a ~$25M 2026 recovery headwind; management calls it timing, but it is fresh and not fully understood. The genuine terminal risk is structural: if AI erodes entry-level graduate employment, repayment weakens on the exact cohort SLM lends to. Insiders show no personal conviction - zero open-market buys against three sellers (68,000 shares). Crucially, the stock is not a bargain on most measures: it trades ABOVE the blended model fair value (~$19) and above the Buffett estimate (~$19), with discounted-cash-flow and intrinsic-value models flashing deeply negative margin of safety; only backward-looking Graham and owner-earnings screens show upside. At $26 the stock already prices the good news and sits only slightly below the freshest analyst targets ($28-29). consensus_delta: For a deep-value name the test is whether the street is pricing terminal decline into stable/growing earnings power - and here it is NOT. interrogator_dossier:
# SLM Corporation (Sallie Mae) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Live price $25.995 (Nasdaq, USD) as of 2026-08-02. Six consecutive earnings calls reviewed: Q2 2025 through Q2 2026.*

Sallie Mae is the largest private student lender in the United States — a deposit-funded bank that originates loans to undergraduates, graduate students and their parents, then increasingly sells those loans to partners for a gain and a recurring fee. The story management is telling is a genuine one: a once-in-a-generation change in federal law is handing them a large new market, and they are re-plumbing the business to be more fee-based and capital-light. The job here is to test that story against the hard numbers.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across the six calls the story has widened from "steady lender buying back its own stock" to "steady lender with a large, legislated growth runway and a new fee engine."

- **The constant (all six calls):** disciplined underwriting (cosigner rate rising from ~80% in Q2 2025 to ~95% on new originations by 2026; average FICO at approval ~754-756) and an aggressive, programmatic buyback. By Q2 2026 management says it has retired roughly 59% of the shares outstanding since 2020 at an average price of about $17.19 — well below today's $26.
- **The new growth driver (introduced Q2 2025, amplified since):** the federal reform bill (H.R.1, signed July 2025) caps Parent PLUS borrowing and eliminates Grad PLUS. Management sizes the resulting private-lending opportunity at "$4.5 billion to $5 billion" of incremental annual originations "when fully phased in" — which it frames as roughly 70% origination growth over several years. This is the load-bearing element of the bull case.
- **The second new driver (Q3 2025 onward):** a "first-of-its-kind" strategic partnership (disclosed as KKR) that buys newly originated loans on a forward-flow basis, generating gain-on-sale plus recurring program-management and servicing fees. This is the "capital-light" pivot — management explicitly wants to "build more recurring fee-based revenue over time."
- **What quietly got harder (Q1-Q2 2026):** net interest margin (the spread the bank earns) compressed to a 4.75% trough in Q2 2026 on excess liquidity from a March loan sale; and a new, specific credit wrinkle appeared — "third-party debt resolution providers" pushing willing-and-able borrowers straight to default. Management frames both as temporary/timing.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Solid, growing results / momentum" | Revenue crept from $2.99B (2024) to $3.11B (2025), ~+4%. Net income $608M → $745M. | **Matches, modestly.** Top line grows low-single-digits; this is a steady lender, not a grower — yet. |
| Buyback is value-accretive | Shares down ~59% since 2020 at ~$17.19 avg; 2026 year-to-date ~13M shares (6.5% of the float) at ~$21.95. | **Verified and genuinely well-timed** — they lean in during price dislocations (the Q1 2026 $200M accelerated repurchase at ~$21.50). |
| EPS growth is strong | GAAP EPS: 2021 $3.61 → 2022 $1.76 → 2023 $2.41 → 2024 $2.68 → 2025 $3.46. Five-year EPS CAGR is **−1.1%**; TTM EPS $3.57. | **Poorer than the headline.** EPS is only now back near its 2021 level, and 2021 was inflated by a post-COVID reserve release. The rise is powered heavily by the shrinking share count and by lumpy loan-sale gains, not organic earnings compounding. Book value per share compounded far better (+15.2% over five years). |
| Credit is healthy / "manageable" | Q2 2026 net charge-offs $113M vs $94M a year earlier; delinquencies 3.7% (down from 4.0% in Q1); reserve rate 5.89%. | **Mixed.** Charge-offs are rising and a new default channel ("debt resolution" firms) cost roughly $16M of the year-over-year increase and a ~$25M 2026 recovery headwind. Management calls it concentrated and timing-related; that is plausible but unproven. |
| Earnings power intact despite the quarter | Q2 2026 GAAP EPS was just **$0.29, missing the ~$0.46 consensus**; net interest income fell $44M year-over-year; NIM 4.75%. | **The weakest data point in the file.** Management attributes it to a liquidity drag it expects to reverse (NIM back toward 5% by year-end). The market looked through the miss — the stock held near $26 — but the quarter was genuinely soft. |

Bottom line: the narrative is slightly *richer* than the trailing financials justify (flat five-year EPS, a headline miss), but the forward story rests on a real, legislated market expansion that the trailing numbers cannot yet show.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY — **Rising**

- Q2 2025: measured, even slightly defensive on volume ("a delayed peak season," nontraditional-school "challenges").
- Q3 2025 / Q4 2025: distinctly more confident — "successful quarter and peak season," the KKR partnership unveiled, a new two-year $500M buyback authorization, and a forward reach to 2027 ("high teens to low 20s" EPS growth potential).
- Q1-Q2 2026: confident on strategy and PLUS-reform readiness ("all of the additional products... delivered," application trends "at the higher end of our expectations or better"), while carefully lowering expectations on near-term margin and flagging the credit wrinkle. The shift is from *defending* volume toward *investing* for growth — an offensive posture — but paired with honest hedging on credit and NIM.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — **Medium-High**

Management has largely delivered. In Q3 2025 it guided full-year 2025 GAAP EPS to $3.20-$3.30; the year came in at $3.46, a beat. It reaffirmed net-charge-off and expense metrics repeatedly and hit them. Against that, the screener records a beat in only 3 of the last 7 quarters (43%) — and Q2 2026 was a clear miss versus the Street — so the quarter-to-quarter print is lumpy even if the annual guide is reliable. There is a mild sandbagging pattern on annual EPS (guide low on loan-sale timing, then beat). Reliability on the things they control (expenses, capital return, underwriting) is high; reliability on quarterly EPS optics is low because loan-sale gains and CECL provisioning swing the number.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Credit, relentlessly.** Every call, analysts press on delinquencies, roll rates and the loan-modification programs ("the noise is deafening on consumer health," RBC, Q3 2025). Management's answer is consistent — late-stage delinquencies and roll rates are stable, 80%+ of modified borrowers keep paying — but the new "debt-resolution" default channel in Q2 2026 is exactly the kind of surprise this line of questioning was probing for.
- **Metric comparability.** Analysts (JPMorgan, Q4 2025 and Q1 2026) keep asking how loan sales distort the reported charge-off and delinquency ratios. Management added a non-GAAP appendix to bridge it — transparent, but it signals the reported ratios are now genuinely harder to read.
- **Gain-on-sale durability and NIM.** Repeated questions on whether gain-on-sale margins and the medium-term ~5% NIM target hold as the mix shifts to graduate loans. Management declines to commit until it sees a full peak season — a reasonable but unresolved open item.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Q2 2026 EPS of $0.29 missed consensus (~$0.46) on falling net interest income and rising expenses.
🔴 Flat five-year EPS; growth is buyback- and gain-on-sale-assisted, not organic compounding.
🔴 A new default channel (third-party "debt resolution" firms) is pushing able borrowers to default — small so far (~$16M) but a fresh, not-fully-understood leak.
🔴 Open-market insider activity is negative: zero buys against three sellers (68,000 shares) — no personal conviction behind the buyback.
🔴 Reported credit ratios now require a non-GAAP bridge to interpret — reduced transparency, even if well-explained.

🟢 A real, legislated growth runway: PLUS reform could lift originations ~70% over several years, and Q2 2026 early peak-season indicators are "at the higher end of expectations or better."
🟢 Genuinely disciplined, counter-cyclical buyback (~59% of shares retired at ~$17, leaning in near $21-22 lows).
🟢 Improving origination quality (cosigner ~95%, FICO ~755) into a growth push — they are not buying volume with credit.
🟢 A building fee engine (program-management + servicing fees up >50% year-over-year off a small base) that lowers capital intensity.
🟢 Strong capital (CET1 11.8%) and a clean Piotroski score of 8/9.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary shifted from "loan sales" (episodic, seasoned-portfolio) to "forward flow" and "strategic partnership" (recurring, new-origination) — a deliberate re-framing of the business model toward fee income, not just balance-sheet spread.
- Management increasingly separates "the bank balance sheet" from "how we fund the business," signalling it intends to grow originations faster than the balance sheet — capital-light by design.
- On the AI-and-jobs worry (a real terminal risk for a student lender, since it threatens graduates' ability to repay), management flips it into a tailwind: "As AI transforms the professional landscape, we believe education will be even more important." That is a narrative choice worth watching against actual recent-graduate delinquency data over the next several quarters.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director) — **STRENGTHENING**

Capital allocation here is a genuine strength: a well-timed, counter-cyclical buyback that has compounded per-share value, funded by a disciplined, high-return lending book that is pivoting toward recurring fees. The trajectory is strengthening because a legislated market expansion (PLUS reform) sits on top of a franchise that is simultaneously improving credit quality and lowering capital intensity.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is a consumer-credit lender heading into a higher-for-longer, late-cycle regime, and the entire *upside* case depends on the PLUS-reform origination ramp actually converting during the first peak season now underway — while the entire *downside* case is a credit turn (the new debt-resolution default channel plus any recent-graduate employment weakness). At $26 the stock already trades above most model-based fair values and offers only a modest discount to the freshest analyst targets, so the risk/reward is a question of *entry price*, not of franchise quality.

**Moat:** a narrow but real moat — scale as the dominant private student lender, the Sallie Mae brand, and preferred-lender relationships with more than 2,100 schools, reinforced by a proprietary underwriting dataset. Returns are high (ROE ~34%) but flattered by thin equity and loan-sale gains, and ROIC (~8.7%) is ordinary; margins are stable, not expanding. That reads as narrow-and-stable, not widening. **Secular threat:** manageable. The dominant structural force — federal reform — is a *tailwind* (private capital steps in where Grad PLUS was removed); the genuine structural risk is AI-driven erosion of entry-level graduate employment impairing repayment, which is real but, on the evidence so far, contained by 90%+ cosigner rates and stable roll rates. The cheapness is best read as a late-cycle credit-lender discount, not a value trap over a melting base.

# SLM Corporation (Sallie Mae) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Live price $25.995 (Nasdaq, USD) as of 2026-08-02. Six consecutive earnings calls reviewed: Q2 2025 through Q2 2026.*

Sallie Mae is the largest private student lender in the United States — a deposit-funded bank that originates loans to undergraduates, graduate students and their parents, then increasingly sells those loans to partners for a gain and a recurring fee. The story management is telling is a genuine one: a once-in-a-generation change in federal law is handing them a large new market, and they are re-plumbing the business to be more fee-based and capital-light. The job here is to test that story against the hard numbers.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Across the six calls the story has widened from "steady lender buying back its own stock" to "steady lender with a large, legislated growth runway and a new fee engine."

- **The constant (all six calls):** disciplined underwriting (cosigner rate rising from ~80% in Q2 2025 to ~95% on new originations by 2026; average FICO at approval ~754-756) and an aggressive, programmatic buyback. By Q2 2026 management says it has retired roughly 59% of the shares outstanding since 2020 at an average price of about $17.19 — well below today's $26.
- **The new growth driver (introduced Q2 2025, amplified since):** the federal reform bill (H.R.1, signed July 2025) caps Parent PLUS borrowing and eliminates Grad PLUS. Management sizes the resulting private-lending opportunity at "$4.5 billion to $5 billion" of incremental annual originations "when fully phased in" — which it frames as roughly 70% origination growth over several years. This is the load-bearing element of the bull case.
- **The second new driver (Q3 2025 onward):** a "first-of-its-kind" strategic partnership (disclosed as KKR) that buys newly originated loans on a forward-flow basis, generating gain-on-sale plus recurring program-management and servicing fees. This is the "capital-light" pivot — management explicitly wants to "build more recurring fee-based revenue over time."
- **What quietly got harder (Q1-Q2 2026):** net interest margin (the spread the bank earns) compressed to a 4.75% trough in Q2 2026 on excess liquidity from a March loan sale; and a new, specific credit wrinkle appeared — "third-party debt resolution providers" pushing willing-and-able borrowers straight to default. Management frames both as temporary/timing.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Solid, growing results / momentum" | Revenue crept from $2.99B (2024) to $3.11B (2025), ~+4%. Net income $608M → $745M. | **Matches, modestly.** Top line grows low-single-digits; this is a steady lender, not a grower — yet. |
| Buyback is value-accretive | Shares down ~59% since 2020 at ~$17.19 avg; 2026 year-to-date ~13M shares (6.5% of the float) at ~$21.95. | **Verified and genuinely well-timed** — they lean in during price dislocations (the Q1 2026 $200M accelerated repurchase at ~$21.50). |
| EPS growth is strong | GAAP EPS: 2021 $3.61 → 2022 $1.76 → 2023 $2.41 → 2024 $2.68 → 2025 $3.46. Five-year EPS CAGR is **−1.1%**; TTM EPS $3.57. | **Poorer than the headline.** EPS is only now back near its 2021 level, and 2021 was inflated by a post-COVID reserve release. The rise is powered heavily by the shrinking share count and by lumpy loan-sale gains, not organic earnings compounding. Book value per share compounded far better (+15.2% over five years). |
| Credit is healthy / "manageable" | Q2 2026 net charge-offs $113M vs $94M a year earlier; delinquencies 3.7% (down from 4.0% in Q1); reserve rate 5.89%. | **Mixed.** Charge-offs are rising and a new default channel ("debt resolution" firms) cost roughly $16M of the year-over-year increase and a ~$25M 2026 recovery headwind. Management calls it concentrated and timing-related; that is plausible but unproven. |
| Earnings power intact despite the quarter | Q2 2026 GAAP EPS was just **$0.29, missing the ~$0.46 consensus**; net interest income fell $44M year-over-year; NIM 4.75%. | **The weakest data point in the file.** Management attributes it to a liquidity drag it expects to reverse (NIM back toward 5% by year-end). The market looked through the miss — the stock held near $26 — but the quarter was genuinely soft. |

Bottom line: the narrative is slightly *richer* than the trailing financials justify (flat five-year EPS, a headline miss), but the forward story rests on a real, legislated market expansion that the trailing numbers cannot yet show.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY — **Rising**

- Q2 2025: measured, even slightly defensive on volume ("a delayed peak season," nontraditional-school "challenges").
- Q3 2025 / Q4 2025: distinctly more confident — "successful quarter and peak season," the KKR partnership unveiled, a new two-year $500M buyback authorization, and a forward reach to 2027 ("high teens to low 20s" EPS growth potential).
- Q1-Q2 2026: confident on strategy and PLUS-reform readiness ("all of the additional products... delivered," application trends "at the higher end of our expectations or better"), while carefully lowering expectations on near-term margin and flagging the credit wrinkle. The shift is from *defending* volume toward *investing* for growth — an offensive posture — but paired with honest hedging on credit and NIM.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — **Medium-High**

Management has largely delivered. In Q3 2025 it guided full-year 2025 GAAP EPS to $3.20-$3.30; the year came in at $3.46, a beat. It reaffirmed net-charge-off and expense metrics repeatedly and hit them. Against that, the screener records a beat in only 3 of the last 7 quarters (43%) — and Q2 2026 was a clear miss versus the Street — so the quarter-to-quarter print is lumpy even if the annual guide is reliable. There is a mild sandbagging pattern on annual EPS (guide low on loan-sale timing, then beat). Reliability on the things they control (expenses, capital return, underwriting) is high; reliability on quarterly EPS optics is low because loan-sale gains and CECL provisioning swing the number.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Credit, relentlessly.** Every call, analysts press on delinquencies, roll rates and the loan-modification programs ("the noise is deafening on consumer health," RBC, Q3 2025). Management's answer is consistent — late-stage delinquencies and roll rates are stable, 80%+ of modified borrowers keep paying — but the new "debt-resolution" default channel in Q2 2026 is exactly the kind of surprise this line of questioning was probing for.
- **Metric comparability.** Analysts (JPMorgan, Q4 2025 and Q1 2026) keep asking how loan sales distort the reported charge-off and delinquency ratios. Management added a non-GAAP appendix to bridge it — transparent, but it signals the reported ratios are now genuinely harder to read.
- **Gain-on-sale durability and NIM.** Repeated questions on whether gain-on-sale margins and the medium-term ~5% NIM target hold as the mix shifts to graduate loans. Management declines to commit until it sees a full peak season — a reasonable but unresolved open item.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Q2 2026 EPS of $0.29 missed consensus (~$0.46) on falling net interest income and rising expenses.
🔴 Flat five-year EPS; growth is buyback- and gain-on-sale-assisted, not organic compounding.
🔴 A new default channel (third-party "debt resolution" firms) is pushing able borrowers to default — small so far (~$16M) but a fresh, not-fully-understood leak.
🔴 Open-market insider activity is negative: zero buys against three sellers (68,000 shares) — no personal conviction behind the buyback.
🔴 Reported credit ratios now require a non-GAAP bridge to interpret — reduced transparency, even if well-explained.

🟢 A real, legislated growth runway: PLUS reform could lift originations ~70% over several years, and Q2 2026 early peak-season indicators are "at the higher end of expectations or better."
🟢 Genuinely disciplined, counter-cyclical buyback (~59% of shares retired at ~$17, leaning in near $21-22 lows).
🟢 Improving origination quality (cosigner ~95%, FICO ~755) into a growth push — they are not buying volume with credit.
🟢 A building fee engine (program-management + servicing fees up >50% year-over-year off a small base) that lowers capital intensity.
🟢 Strong capital (CET1 11.8%) and a clean Piotroski score of 8/9.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- The vocabulary shifted from "loan sales" (episodic, seasoned-portfolio) to "forward flow" and "strategic partnership" (recurring, new-origination) — a deliberate re-framing of the business model toward fee income, not just balance-sheet spread.
- Management increasingly separates "the bank balance sheet" from "how we fund the business," signalling it intends to grow originations faster than the balance sheet — capital-light by design.
- On the AI-and-jobs worry (a real terminal risk for a student lender, since it threatens graduates' ability to repay), management flips it into a tailwind: "As AI transforms the professional landscape, we believe education will be even more important." That is a narrative choice worth watching against actual recent-graduate delinquency data over the next several quarters.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director) — **STRENGTHENING**

Capital allocation here is a genuine strength: a well-timed, counter-cyclical buyback that has compounded per-share value, funded by a disciplined, high-return lending book that is pivoting toward recurring fees. The trajectory is strengthening because a legislated market expansion (PLUS reform) sits on top of a franchise that is simultaneously improving credit quality and lowering capital intensity.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is a consumer-credit lender heading into a higher-for-longer, late-cycle regime, and the entire *upside* case depends on the PLUS-reform origination ramp actually converting during the first peak season now underway — while the entire *downside* case is a credit turn (the new debt-resolution default channel plus any recent-graduate employment weakness). At $26 the stock already trades above most model-based fair values and offers only a modest discount to the freshest analyst targets, so the risk/reward is a question of *entry price*, not of franchise quality.

**Moat:** a narrow but real moat — scale as the dominant private student lender, the Sallie Mae brand, and preferred-lender relationships with more than 2,100 schools, reinforced by a proprietary underwriting dataset. Returns are high (ROE ~34%) but flattered by thin equity and loan-sale gains, and ROIC (~8.7%) is ordinary; margins are stable, not expanding. That reads as narrow-and-stable, not widening. **Secular threat:** manageable. The dominant structural force — federal reform — is a *tailwind* (private capital steps in where Grad PLUS was removed); the genuine structural risk is AI-driven erosion of entry-level graduate employment impairing repayment, which is real but, on the evidence so far, contained by 90%+ cosigner rates and stable roll rates. The cheapness is best read as a late-cycle credit-lender discount, not a value trap over a melting base.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 4 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable

bull_thesis: Sallie Mae is the largest US private student lender and is gaining share at the moment its market is getting bigger. Federal PLUS reform, which caps federal graduate and parent loans from July 2026, is already showing in the numbers: third-quarter 2026 originations were a record $3.4 billion (up 15%), graduate originations rose 119% with FICO credit scores about 9 points above the book average, and October disbursements were up 35% month to date. Management estimates the reform could eventually add $4.5-5 billion a year, roughly 70% more than 2025 volume. Funding that growth no longer depends only on the bank balance sheet. A second partner, Sixth Street, committed on 2026-10-22 to buy at least $1.5 billion of new loans a year for three years, on top of the KKR arrangement from late 2025, and both pay recurring program-management and servicing fees (other income up $15 million year on year in Q3 2026). The third-quarter loss of $0.19 a share is largely accounting timing. CECL (the current expected credit loss standard) requires a lender to reserve for a loan's lifetime losses on the day it is made, so record originations brought $214 million of provisions in the quarter, while the planned whole-loan sale that would have booked gains was postponed. Underneath, credit outside one segment is stable: the reserve rate is 5.89%, down year on year, co-signers back about 95% of new loans, and borrowers leaving loan-modification programs are performing better than planned. The extra losses come from borrowers steered into default by debt-resolution firms, and management says those borrowers can pay, with early recoveries running at meaningfully higher rates. If 2027 earnings come in near the street's $3.00 a share (2028: $3.65), the stock at $16.55 trades at about 5.5 times next year's earnings and about 1.5 times book value of roughly $10.8 a share. For a franchise that earned more than 25% on equity in 2025 and has cut its share count 59% since 2020, that is cheap. Book value also understates the loans, which have been selling at mid- to high single-digit gains over a carrying value already net of a roughly 6% reserve. Conditions: fourth-quarter 2026 charge-offs land inside the $400-420 million full-year guide, 2027 guidance implies a clear rebound in earnings per share, and loan-sale premiums recover as rate volatility eases.
bear_thesis: The 2026 reset is a credibility event and possibly the first chapter of a broader credit turn, not a one-off. In twelve months management went from 'not observed any material change in our borrowers' ability' (2025-10-23), to a $25 million debt-resolution hit 'concentrated, understood and manageable' (2026-07-23), to a $45 million hit, a net charge-off guide of $400-420 million against an original $345-385 million, and an earnings-per-share guide cut about 36% to $1.95-2.05 (2026-10-22). Loans 30 or more days delinquent were 4.2% against 4.0% a year earlier, and forbearance rose to 2.3% from 2.0%. The 2026 graduating class enters repayment this fall, with entry-level hiring under pressure from AI, and management admits it cannot see more than about twelve months ahead on credit. The hidden value in the loans, the main bull argument, just failed its test: the planned roughly $1 billion whole-loan sale was cancelled because higher long-term rates pushed premiums below the company's threshold. In the current backdrop of positive real rates and a steep yield curve, fixed-rate student loans are worth less to buyers, and that may last. Capital is thinning. Common equity is about $2.0 billion, the core capital ratio slipped to 11.8% at Q2 2026 from 12.4% at Q1, and the company spent heavily on buybacks at $22-26 a share this year with only $111 million of authorization left, so the buyback that supported the stock is close to exhausted just as growth needs capital. Expenses are running at $750-780 million a year to compete for graduate loans, and pricing pressure in that market is building. Three law firms opened shareholder investigations in late October, and insiders sold 68,000 shares with no purchases. The stock has fallen to a new 52-week low ($16.39 intraday on 2026-11-16) and keeps falling after a 2026-10-23 drop. If 2027 earnings land near $2.00 a share, which is plausible if charge-offs keep running above $420 million and sale gains stay small, 6 times earnings gives about $12, or about 1.1 times book. Confirmation would be: fourth-quarter charge-offs above guidance, a 30+ day delinquency rate above 4.5% in early 2027, 2027 guidance below about $2.25 a share, or another cancelled or sub-par loan sale.
consensus_delta: The street is split (11 firms: 5 buy, 5 hold, 1 sell) and still anchored high. The consensus target is $25.67, and the four October targets averaged $24.50, 48% above today's price. 2027 consensus earnings per share are $3.00 and 2028 $3.65, which assumes 2026 was purely timing (CECL reserves on record growth plus a delayed sale) and that earnings bounce back about 50% next year. We agree that part of the Q3 loss is accounting timing, but we think the street is too quick to treat the debt-resolution losses and the sale premium as fixed. Charge-off guidance has moved twice in two quarters, and premiums depend on long-term rates that the macro backdrop says will stay positive and volatile. The market at $16.55 prices 2027 earnings nearer $2.00-2.25 at a distrusted multiple. Our base case of about $2.65 sits between the two. Where we disagree with the market: the franchise and growth are better than the share price implies, while the earnings path is worse than the street targets imply. The stock is cheap, but it is not yet safe.
forcing_function: In order: (1) the CEO's fireside chat at TD Cowen on 2026-11-17, the first public comment since the reset, likely with an update on peak season and debt-resolution recoveries; (2) the 'insights … later this fall' on the size of the PLUS opportunity, promised on 2026-10-22; (3) the decisive one, the fourth-quarter 2026 results with full-year charge-offs and 2027 guidance, expected around 2027-01-21. A 2027 guide pointing to $2.60 a share or more with charge-offs inside $400-420 million would restore the earnings-power thesis and should send the multiple back toward 8 times. Further out, a resumed whole-loan sale at a normal premium, a new buyback authorization, or a third strategic partner for graduate loans (management's stated next priority, before the 2027 peak season) would each give the market a dated reason to re-rate.
valley_of_death: The risky window is the next three months. (1) The 2026 graduating class enters repayment between November 2026 and January 2027, when stress on young borrowers is seasonally highest, while entry-level hiring is soft. (2) Fourth-quarter numbers will carry more CECL reserves on elevated October disbursements (up 35%), and gains depend on closing the rest of the $600 million Sixth Street seed portfolio and the KKR flow sale of about $1.44 billion of loans held for sale. (3) The buyback is nearly exhausted ($111 million left at 2026-09-30), so the steady daily bid on the shares fades just as tax-loss selling peaks in November and December. (4) Shareholder-investigation headlines may turn into a filed class action. There is no debt wall or liquidity risk: the bank is deposit-funded, with liquidity at 18.6% of assets and total risk-based capital of 13.1% at Q2 2026. The risk is a lower earnings base, not solvency.
positioning_washout: Forced-selling pressure is moderate and mostly behavioral, not contractual. The stock has fallen about 47% from its $31.06 high and sits at a new 52-week low ($16.39 intraday on 2026-11-16), about 28% below its 200-day average. Growth-at-a-reasonable-price and momentum holders who bought the PLUS-reform story are likely leaving, along with tax-loss sellers of 2026 purchases made at $22-26. No index deletion or dividend cut forces sales: the $0.13 quarterly dividend was maintained on 2026-10-20 and is covered. Insiders sold 68,000 shares in the open market with no purchases. We do not name a price-wait level, because no identifiable forced seller is due at a specific level. The question is whether the thesis holds, not where a flush ends.
moderator_conclusion: Wait for proof: we buy once the fourth-quarter 2026 results, due around 2027-01-21, show full-year 2026 charge-offs at or below $420 million and 2027 earnings guidance of at least about $2.60 a share. The thesis is in doubt until that test. The business case is half proven. The growth half holds: record originations of $3.4 billion in the third quarter, graduate lending up 119%, and a second partner (Sixth Street) committing at least $1.5 billion a year all show that federal PLUS reform is handing Sallie Mae a bigger market. The earnings half has not held. On 2026-10-22 the company reported a $0.19 per share loss, raised its charge-off guidance for the second time, cancelled a loan sale because buyers' premiums fell with higher rates, and cut 2026 earnings guidance by about 36%, three months after calling the higher figure achievable. At $16.55 the stock prices much of that, at about 1.5 times book value and about 5.5 times the street's 2027 earnings. Our base fair value is $21 (8 times about $2.65 of 2027 earnings, cross-checked against adjusted book value), about 27% above today, against a downside case of about $12 if 2027 earnings settle near $2. That is roughly one-to-one with no structural floor, which is not enough to buy ahead of proof from a team whose forecasts just missed badly. The macro backdrop (positive real long rates, fearful credit) is a headwind for a lender whose hidden value depends on selling fixed-rate loans, though that is context, not the reason for waiting. Conviction is middling. The franchise, its narrow but real moat (scale, more than 2,100 school relationships, cheap deposit funding) and the share count cut by 59% since 2020 make this worth owning if credit stabilizes. A management team scored at 2 of 5 for credibility, deteriorating earnings delivery and a buyback nearly spent are why we wait for the January numbers instead of paying for the promise now.
sop_breakdown: Base case, per share, in US dollars on about 185 million shares. Earnings power: 2027 earnings per share of about $2.65, a haircut of roughly 12% to the street's $3.00 for a further rise in charge-offs and smaller sale gains, at 8 times earnings gives about $21.2. Asset cross-check: tangible common equity of about $10.5 a share, plus a reduced loan-book premium of about 4 cents per dollar after tax (about $3.3 a share, reflecting the higher-rate premium environment that caused the sale to be cancelled), gives an adjusted book of about $13.8. At 1.5 times, for a high-teens return on equity, that is about $20.7. Reconciled base fair value: $21. Funding debt is inside equity and is not subtracted again, and there are no pending special distributions (the $0.13 quarterly common dividend is ordinary). The base case assumes the business gets back toward its long-run economics over the 18-month horizon.
risk_reward: From $16.55: the downside price is $12.0 (about $4.55 lower) and fair value is $21.0 (about $4.45 higher), close to one-to-one. There is no structural floor, because a bank's book value can be eroded by losses. The pipeline computes the exact ratios from these levels.
peer_comps_note: The peer file (NAVI, NNI, SYF, ALLY, COF, AXP, ENVA) rates Sallie Mae cheap against its peers but gives no live anchor multiple, so this note quotes no peer multiple from memory. Our own check: at $16.55 the stock trades at about 5.5 times 2027 consensus earnings and about 8 times the bottom of 2026 guidance ($1.95-2.05), and at about 1.5 times book value of roughly $10.8 a share. The peer file's support for 'cheap' leans on the Graham, owner-earnings and earnings-power models, which use industrial cash-flow measures that suit a bank poorly. Its point that the market is pricing credit and policy risk is right. The discount is mostly name-specific (a 36% guidance cut, cancelled sale, debt-resolution losses), not shared sector movement, so it counts as a single-name discount, with a credibility cost the company earned. Peer position: cheap against peers, by a margin that pays for the doubt but does not remove it.
interrogator_dossier:
# Sallie Mae (SLM) — a deep dive on management and the setup
*Five earnings calls, October 2025 to October 2026, tested against the reported numbers. Prepared 2026-11-16, with the stock at $16.55 (Nasdaq, US dollars), a new 52-week low and down about 47% from its $31.06 high.*

**The takeaway.** Sallie Mae, the largest private student lender in the US, has executed the growth half of its story well: record originations and two new funding partners. It has missed on the earnings half. Over twelve months management kept saying that credit was "stable" and that its loans were worth more than the share price implied. Then on 2026-10-22 it reported a quarterly loss of $0.19 a share, raised its 2026 charge-off guidance for the second time, and cut 2026 earnings-per-share guidance by more than a third, to $1.95–$2.05 from $3.10–$3.20, three months after the finance chief described a "viable path" to the higher figure. The franchise holds up. Management's forecasting has not.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

- **Q3 2025 (2025-10-23): credit is fine, buy the dip.** The message was "a successful quarter and peak season". Net charge-offs (loans written off as uncollectable, net of recoveries) were 1.95% of loans in repayment, and management said it had "not observed any material change in our borrowers' ability to meet their obligations". It bought back 5.6 million shares at $29.45 and promised a "first-of-its-kind" private-credit partnership.
- **Q4 2025 (2026-01-22): the new model.** The KKR partnership launched. Sallie Mae now sells newly originated loans to a partner for a fee instead of keeping them all on its own balance sheet. Management said federal PLUS reform (caps on federal graduate and parent loans) could add about $5 billion of yearly originations, roughly 70% growth over 2025 when fully phased in. It flagged that the new sale mechanics would distort reported credit ratios and added non-GAAP versions of them (figures that do not follow standard accounting rules). The market sold off on the softer earnings path. The CEO pointed to "high teens to low 20s" earnings growth in 2027.
- **Q1 2026 (2026-04-23): exploit the gap.** Earnings per share were $1.54. Management sold a $2 billion seasoned portfolio at "mid- to high single-digit" gains and launched a $200 million accelerated share repurchase (a buyback in which a bank delivers the shares up front). The stated reason was "the disconnect between the premium from our whole loan sales and our equity valuation". This was the high point of confidence.
- **Q2 2026 (2026-07-23): a new credit problem appears.** Earnings per share fell to $0.29. Management disclosed borrowers who "have both the willingness and capacity to repay" but were going straight to default after signing up with debt-resolution firms. It suspended many recovery efforts, estimated a $25 million hit, and said the hit would fit inside guidance.
- **Q3 2026 (2026-10-22): growth delivered, earnings pulled.** Originations reached a record $3.4 billion (up 15%), graduate originations rose 119%, and a second partner, Sixth Street, committed to buy at least $1.5 billion a year. Against that, the company lost money for the quarter, raised the debt-resolution hit to $45 million, lifted net charge-off guidance to $400–$420 million, and cancelled a planned whole-loan sale because higher long-term rates had pushed the price buyers offered below its threshold.

Over the year the story widened from "a high-return bank buying back stock" to "a lender plus a fee-earning loan manager, growing faster because of PLUS reform". The proof that the loans are worth more than book value, which a sale delivers, has stalled exactly when it was needed.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | What the numbers show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Credit is stable, losses in the "high 1s to low 2s" (Q1 2026) | 2025 net charge-offs were $346 million (2.15%). 2026 guidance went from $345–$385M, to the upper end (Q2), to $400–$420M (Q3), about 16% above the original midpoint. Loans 30+ days delinquent were 4.2% at Q3 2026, up from 4.0% a year earlier, and forbearance rose to 2.3% from 2.0% | Worse than the narrative. The rise is attributed to a "small segment", but the guidance moved twice |
| Loans are worth more than the stock implies; sale premiums of about 106–107 cents per dollar of loans | Q1 2026 sales booked $146M of gains on $3.3B plus $131M of reserve release. Gains fell to $3.7M in Q3 2026 against $136M a year earlier, after the planned sale was cancelled on price | The value is real but depends on rates. It cannot be counted at the Q1 premium |
| PLUS reform means 70% more originations over several years | Q3 2026 originations were up 15%, graduate originations up 119%, October disbursements up 35% month to date, full-year guidance of 12–14% growth held | Matches the narrative |
| Fee revenue from partnerships builds | Other income was $45–46M a quarter (up $15–16M year on year) | Matches, from a small base |
| 2026 earnings per share of $3.10–$3.20, with a "viable path" to the higher figure (Q2) | Now $1.95–$2.05. Year to date: $1.54 + $0.29 − $0.19 = $1.64 | A clear miss |
| Disciplined, value-creating buybacks | Shares are down about 59% since 2020 at an average of $17.19. 2026 buybacks so far averaged about $22–26 (Q3: 5.1M shares at $25.69), against a stock now at $16.55. About $111M of authorization was left at 2026-09-30, and common equity fell to about $2.0B (around $10.8 a share) | Good over the long run, poorly timed in 2026 |

A note on the screener figures. The "net margin 24%", "ROIC 8.7%", P/FCF 6.2x (price to free cash flow) and "net debt" numbers are industrial ratios that do not describe a bank. Free cash flow for a lender is mostly loan-sale timing, and its "debt" is funding, not leverage. This analysis does not rely on them.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY — Declining (from offensive to defensive)

- Q3 2025: "real momentum that will carry us through the rest of the year."
- Q4 2025: "high teens to low 20s" earnings growth in 2027.
- Q1 2026: "capable of performing in almost any environment."
- Q2 2026: "the current loss pressure is concentrated, understood and manageable."
- Q3 2026: "While we would prefer a different macroeconomic environment…" and "how our outlook has evolved".

Guidance has become less specific. The CEO now says he cannot see more than about twelve months ahead on credit, and 2027 talk has moved from a growth range to "we look forward to sharing our insights … later this fall."

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — Low

Origination guidance has been met every quarter (2025: $7.4B, up 6%, at the top of the revised range; 2026: 12–14% held). Earnings and charge-off guidance has not: the 2025 EPS guide was reset lower in October 2025 because of loan-sale timing, the 2026 charge-off guide was raised twice, and the 2026 EPS guide was cut about 36%. Our scan shows estimates beaten in only 3 of 7 quarters (43%). There is no pattern of setting a low bar. Instead, plans that depend on loan sales keep meeting a market that does not cooperate. Three law firms announced shareholder investigations between 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-30. These are advertisements, not lawsuits, but they show how sharp the reset felt.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

- **Delinquency direction:** asked in every call (Orenbuch, Arfstrom). Each time the answer was that it was a seasonal peak, the loan-modification programs are working, or watch late-stage loans instead. The 30+ day rate is still above the year-earlier level.
- **Whether reported ratios still mean anything:** Shane (Q1 and Q3 2026) asked whether loan sales distort charge-off rates and the held-for-sale balance. Management acknowledges the distortion, which makes year-on-year credit comparisons hard for outsiders.
- **Gain-on-sale margins:** asked in Q4 2025 and Q3 2026, with no firm number given. The cancelled sale answers part of the question.
- **Grad loan mix and the net interest margin:** management will not commit until it has seen a full peak season. The long-run target of a "low to mid-5%" margin compares with 4.75–4.85% in Q2–Q3 2026.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

- Red: 2026 EPS guidance cut about 36% on 2026-10-22, three months after the "viable path" comment of 2026-07-23.
- Red: net charge-off guidance raised twice in 2026, and debt-resolution losses grew from $25M to $45M within one quarter.
- Red: the planned whole-loan sale was cancelled (Q3 2026) because rate volatility pushed premiums below management's threshold, the same premium management had cited to justify the buyback.
- Red: shares were bought at about $22–26 in 2026 and the stock is now $16.55. The buyback budget is nearly spent ($111M left) as capital ratios slip (CET1, the core bank-capital ratio, was 11.8% at Q2 2026 against 12.4% at Q1).
- Red: insiders made 3 open-market sales (68,000 shares) and no buys.
- Green: record originations of $3.4B in Q3 2026, graduate loans up 119% with FICO credit scores about 9 points above the book average, and 95% of new loans with a co-signer.
- Green: a second strategic partner (Sixth Street, at least $1.5B a year for three years, announced 2026-10-22) shows that outside buyers want the loans even after the cancelled sale.
- Green: the loan-modification programs are beating plan, with more than 75% of borrowers who left them still paying after 3 to 6 months (Q2 2026).
- Green: deposit duration was extended to 37 months from 23, leaving the company close to neutral to rate moves (Q3 2026).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- "Misaligned third-party debt resolution practices" is a new phrase for a new kind of loss: borrowers who can pay but are being steered to default. Management's response, suspending outside recoveries and using AI to review calls, shows this is more than noise. "Adoption … has been slower than we initially expected" (Q3 2026) suggests it will spill into 2027.
- The language has moved from "loan sale premium versus equity value" (Q1) to "a more diversified and flexible funding model" (Q3). Management is quietly backing away from one-off portfolio sales as the source of value and leaning on recurring fees.
- Pete Graham is now Co-President as well as CFO, and Melissa Bronaugh has become Deputy CFO, which looks like succession planning. CEO Jon Witter speaks at the TD Cowen conference on 2026-11-17, the first look at management since the reset.
- Q3 2026 provisions (money set aside for expected losses) were $214M, mostly the upfront loss reserve that CECL accounting (the current expected credit loss standard) requires on the record originations. Part of the Q3 loss is that accounting timing, not losses that have already happened. This is the most important point for anyone who sees value here.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: DETERIORATING** in earnings delivery and credibility, despite a stronger franchise and growing volumes.

**The single most important thing to weigh:** whether the 2026 credit and earnings reset is contained (one debt-resolution segment, plus upfront reserves on fast growth, plus one cancelled sale) or the start of a broader rise in losses among young borrowers. The next clean evidence is the Q4 2026 results and 2027 guidance in late January 2027.

**Moat:** narrow and regulatory/scale-based. Sallie Mae is the preferred lender at more than 2,100 schools, funds itself with cheap insured bank deposits, has decades of student-credit data, and has strong co-signer rates. Through-cycle returns on equity have been high (above 25% in 2025 on thin equity), but that partly reflects loan-sale gains. The moat is not widening: competition for graduate loans has added some marketing pressure. Trend: stable.

**Secular threat:** manageable. AI could reduce entry-level jobs for graduates, which is what lets borrowers repay, and federal policy could change again. The opposite force, PLUS reform, is enlarging the market. The cheapness looks like a fear discount on stable-to-growing earnings power plus a credibility discount the company earned. It does not look like a value trap on a shrinking base, but management must show that 2026 was a reset and not a trend.

Management credibility 2 of 5 · trajectory weakening · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.
thesis_evidence: Two load-bearing claims held up on 2026-10-22: growth from PLUS reform (record Q3 2026 originations of $3.4 billion, up 15%, graduate originations up 119%) and partner demand for the loans (Sixth Street, at least $1.5 billion a year). Two are now in doubt. The first is that credit losses are contained. The 2026 net charge-off guide was raised to $400-420 million from $345-385 million, the debt-resolution hit grew to $45 million from $25 million, 30+ day delinquency was 4.2% against 4.0% a year earlier (Q3 2026, reported 2026-10-22), and the 2026 earnings-per-share guide was cut to $1.95-2.05 from $3.10-3.20. The second is that the loans can be sold at a premium to book: the planned roughly $1 billion sale was cancelled in Q3 2026 because premiums fell below the threshold. Neither is disproven. Management attributes the excess losses to one segment and the gain shortfall to timing. The next dated evidence that settles it is the fourth-quarter 2026 results and 2027 guidance.
